lead: A receiver adds its own noise, so the signal-to-noise ratio at its output is lower than at its input. Noise figure and noise temperature state that degradation as a single number. They let an engineer compare amplifiers, choose the first stage of a receiver, and predict the SNR that reaches the demodulator. The idea is used in satellite receivers, mobile handsets, Wi-Fi front ends and radio astronomy. This chapter defines both measures, connects them, and shows how they combine when stages are cascaded.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for noise power, SNR and AWGN.

blocks.text: Every amplifier adds noise of its own. The signal-to-noise ratio at the input is measured with a source at a stated temperature. The signal-to-noise ratio at the output is measured at the load. The ratio of these two ratios is the noise factor F:

blocks.where: F is the linear noise factor (no unit); SNR<sub>in</sub> is input signal-to-noise ratio as a power ratio; SNR<sub>out</sub> is output signal-to-noise ratio as a power ratio.

blocks.text: F is always at least 1. A noiseless device has F = 1. F is not a gain and is not in decibels. Some syllabi call this linear F the noise factor. The noise figure NF is the same number in decibels:

blocks.where: NF is the noise figure in dB; F is the linear noise factor; log<sub>10</sub> is the base-10 logarithm.

blocks.text: A device with F = 2 has NF = 3.01 dB. Datasheets quote NF in dB because decibels compress a wide range. Formulas use F because noise powers add and gains multiply. The definition needs a source temperature. The standard reference is T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K, about 17 °C. It is a convention, not exactly room temperature. F compares SNR, not output noise power alone.

Noise temperature T<sub>e</sub> is the temperature of a matched resistor at the device input that would produce the same added noise power as the device. The added noise power referred to the input is k T<sub>e</sub> B, where k is Boltzmann's constant, T<sub>e</sub> is in kelvin, and B is the noise bandwidth in hertz. At the output, this added noise power is multiplied by the device power gain G. This is a bookkeeping temperature, not a physical temperature you can touch.

blocks.where: F is the linear noise factor; T<sub>e</sub> is the equivalent noise temperature in kelvin; T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K.
T<sub>e</sub> is the equivalent noise temperature in kelvin; F is the linear noise factor; T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K.

blocks.text: A device with F = 2 has T<sub>e</sub> = 290 K. A low-noise amplifier can have T<sub>e</sub> below 100 K. A lossy cable can have T<sub>e</sub> of several hundred kelvin.

A lossy component is an attenuator or cable with power loss L, where L is input power divided by output power and L ≥ 1. At physical temperature T<sub>0</sub>, its noise factor is F = L and its noise temperature is T<sub>e</sub> = (L − 1)T<sub>0</sub>. A 3 dB loss means L = 2, so F = 2 and T<sub>e</sub> = 290 K. Loss placed before an amplifier raises the overall noise figure.

A receiver is a chain of stages. Stage 1 has linear gain G<sub>1</sub> and linear noise factor F<sub>1</sub>. Stage 2 has G<sub>2</sub> and F<sub>2</sub>. Gains and noise factors must be linear, not in dB. The overall noise factor for two stages is:

blocks.where: F is the overall linear noise factor; F<sub>1</sub>, F<sub>2</sub> are stage noise factors; G<sub>1</sub> is stage 1 linear power gain.

blocks.text: For three stages the formula extends:

blocks.where: F is overall noise factor; F<sub>i</sub> is stage i noise factor; G<sub>i</sub> is stage i linear power gain; the pattern continues for more stages.

blocks.text: The second stage's excess noise F<sub>2</sub> − 1 is divided by G<sub>1</sub>. Stage 1 amplifies the signal and its own noise before stage 2 adds noise. A large G<sub>1</sub> makes the second term small. The first stage dominates the overall noise figure. This is why a receiver puts a low-noise amplifier at the antenna and why loss before that amplifier is costly.

Procedure: convert every NF in dB to F = 10^(NF/10). Convert every gain in dB to G = 10^(G<sub>dB</sub>/10). Put these linear values into Friis. Convert the result back with NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub> F. The figure shows the two-stage chain used in the example.

figure.caption: Stage 1 has the lower noise figure and sets the overall noise. The second stage's noise is divided by the first stage's gain in the Friis formula.

spec.title: Two-stage receiver
spec.aria: An antenna feeds stage 1 with gain 20 dB and noise figure 3 dB, then stage 2 with gain 20 dB and noise figure 6 dB, then the output.

examples.question: A two-stage receiver has stage 1 gain 20 dB and noise figure 3 dB. Stage 2 has gain 20 dB and noise figure 6 dB. The source is at T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K. Find the overall noise factor F, the overall noise figure NF in dB, and the equivalent noise temperature T<sub>e</sub>.
steps: Convert stage 1 noise figure: F<sub>1</sub> = 10^(3/10) = 1.995, taken as 2.00 (linear).
Convert stage 2 noise figure: F<sub>2</sub> = 10^(6/10) = 3.981, taken as 4.00 (linear).
Apply Friis for two stages: F = F<sub>1</sub> + (F<sub>2</sub> − 1)/G<sub>1</sub> = 2 + (4 − 1)/100 = 2 + 0.03 = 2.03.
Convert overall noise factor to dB: NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(2.03) = 3.07 dB.
Find equivalent noise temperature: T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1)T<sub>0</sub> = (2.03 − 1) × 290 = 1.03 × 290 = 298.7 K.
examples.answer: Overall noise factor F = 2.03 (linear), overall noise figure NF = 3.07 dB, and equivalent noise temperature T<sub>e</sub> = 298.7 K.
examples.check:
import math
G1_dB = 20
F1_dB = 3
G2_dB = 20
F2_dB = 6
G1 = 10**(G1_dB/10)
G2 = 10**(G2_dB/10)
F1 = 2.00
F2 = 4.00
F = F1 + (F2 - 1)/G1
NF_dB = 10*math.log10(F)
T0 = 290
Te = (F - 1)*T0
print(f"{F:.2f}")
print(f"{NF_dB:.2f}")
print(f"{Te:.1f}")

traps: Do not add noise figures in dB. Friis needs linear F and linear G. Convert first, apply the formula, then convert back.
The reference temperature is T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K, not 300 K. Using 300 K shifts T<sub>e</sub> and is a common marking error.
F is linear and NF is in dB. F cannot be below 1, so a real device cannot have a negative NF in dB.
A lossy cable is not noiseless. At T<sub>0</sub>, F = L and G = 1/L; loss before the first amplifier can dominate the system noise.
Noise temperature is not the physical temperature of the amplifier. It is the temperature of a matched source that would add the same noise power.

quiz.q: Define noise figure in dB and state the reference temperature used in its definition.
quiz.a: Noise figure NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub> F, where F = SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub> is the linear noise factor. The standard reference temperature is T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K.

quiz.q: Why is the linear noise factor F never less than 1?
quiz.a: Any real device adds noise, so the output SNR cannot be larger than the input SNR. Therefore SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub> ≥ 1. An ideal noiseless device has F = 1.

quiz.q: An amplifier has linear noise factor F = 4. Find its noise figure in dB and its equivalent noise temperature at T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K.
Two stages have F<sub>1</sub> = 1.5, G<sub>1</sub> = 20 dB and F<sub>2</sub> = 3, G<sub>2</sub> = 20 dB. Compute the overall noise factor and explain which stage matters more.
quiz.a: G<sub>1</sub> = 100. F = F<sub>1</sub> + (F<sub>2</sub> − 1)/G<sub>1</sub> = 1.5 + 2/100 = 1.52. Stage 1 matters more because its noise factor 1.5 is close to the overall 1.52; stage 2 adds only 0.02 after division by G<sub>1</sub>.

quiz.q: A 6 dB attenuator at 290 K is placed before an amplifier. Find its linear noise factor and noise temperature.
A receiver has overall linear noise factor F = 1.5. Find its noise figure in dB and its equivalent noise temperature at 290 K.
Why must dB noise figures be converted to linear values before using the Friis formula?
quiz.a: The Friis formula adds noise powers and divides by linear power gains. A dB value is a logarithm, so adding dB values would multiply the underlying ratios, which is not the physical process.

quiz.q: State the Friis formula for three cascaded stages.
quiz.a: F = F<sub>1</sub> + (F<sub>2</sub> − 1)/G<sub>1</sub> + (F<sub>3</sub> − 1)/(G<sub>1</sub>G<sub>2</sub>), where F<sub>i</sub> are linear noise factors and G<sub>i</sub> are linear power gains.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical noise figure is measured with a calibrated noise source and the Y-factor method, which compares output noise power with the source on and off. Satellite low-noise blocks and radio telescopes push the first-stage noise temperature down, sometimes by cooling the amplifier. Modern CMOS receivers are designed with Friis in mind: the first stage gets the gain and the low noise. Search 'Y-factor noise figure measurement', 'cascaded noise figure' and 'cryogenic low-noise amplifier'.
